name: Medical Affairs and Medical Writing
blurb: AI in regulatory and medical writing, evidence dossiers, study reports and promotional review.
title: Medical Affairs and Medical Writing
answer: Medical writers use generative AI to draft and summarise clinical study reports, submission modules and evidence dossiers, and to speed promotional review. Regulators have set no separate pathway for AI written content: the sponsor stays fully accountable for every word submitted.

reading.body:
Medical writers use generative AI for first drafts and summaries, but no regulator has created a separate pathway for AI written content, so the sponsor remains accountable for every word submitted.

The pattern across the sub-topics is consistent: AI enters at the drafting stage, in clinical study reports, submission modules, evidence dossiers and promotional review, while accountability stays with the sponsor. The FDA's draft guidance on AI in drug development keeps responsibility for submitted information with the sponsor and asks for evidence of model credibility where AI produces regulatory data. A review in Clinical and Translational Science reached the same practical conclusion, that human review remains essential.

For AI specifically, this is a governance constraint rather than a compute one. The bottleneck in medical writing is not model capability but traceability, since every statement must trace to source data and the review trail must show who checked it. Citation reliability is a named concern, which is why the working rule is first drafts, summaries and consistency checks, never final authorship.

What the data does not cover is volume. It gives no count of submissions drafted with AI, no error or retraction rates, and no comparison of AI assisted writing against conventional drafting. It also does not say how regulators will treat AI use in practice beyond the sponsor accountability principle, or whether any submission has been rejected over it.
